spec.title: PROP-068 — Transfers: every download as data, sampled, journaled and watchable

status.comment: Drafted 2026-11-01 on the owner's request: an external application must see every download vibe performs, precisely and nearly live, to draw speed graphs; the shell's downloads screen (Architect) consumes it. Architect answered the open points the same day (notes/59 §8.1 p. 8; the shell side is R127): the Activity screen draws NETWORK and PEAK tiles, a per-second speed graph over the last five minutes, the byte line with its own bar and ETA beside the step percentage, and the day's totals from the history.

p.purpose: vibe moves bytes from the network to the machine in several places — the `sources`, `archive` and `native` inputs of an application installer option, the per-package clones a project install and `cache add` bring through a registry, the release bundle of `self update`, the catalog files of an index — and each place reports its own way: a `measurement` on the progress stream at best, with no identity, no timestamp a graph could use, and no trace once the process ends. The owner wants an external application, the desktop shell first, to see every download precisely and nearly live, draw its speed, and keep a record, the way a game store's downloads page does. This document names the transfer as a thing of its own, the samples it produces, where they go while it runs and after, and the verbs that read them.

p.principle: A **transfer** is one stream of bytes from outside the machine to it, with an identity, a purpose, a size when known, and a series of timestamped samples of how many bytes have arrived. Every place vibe downloads goes through one wrapper that produces those samples; the wrapper writes them to two places at once — the progress stream of the running command, for the tool that started it, and a journal under the settings root, for any tool on the machine — so the shell can show what its own runner started and what a terminal started alike. vibe records cumulative bytes and the clock, at a cadence fine enough for a live graph, and beside each sample one rate over the last second and, per transfer, the peak of those rates — conveniences so a detached reader that did not listen from the start sees the same figures a listening one computes; the samples stay the truth, and projections (an ETA) belong to the reader. For a finished transfer it keeps a compact per-second series so a graph can be drawn without having listened.

p.transfer: A transfer has: `id` — `<pid>:<n>`, the process and its running count, unique on the machine for as long as the journal keeps it; `kind` — `http` (a response body vibe reads and counts itself) or `git` (a clone or fetch the git binary performs, whose progress vibe reads from git's own reporting); `url` — the source with credentials, query and fragment removed, never a token; `purpose` — one of the closed vocabulary of `#purpose`; `package` — the package key the bytes are for, when there is one (`org.vibevm.apps/vim@9.1.0`), and `step` — the installer step id, when a step asked; `destination` — `store` (the machine store or the registry cache), `cache` (the application cache of `PROP-065#sources`), `work` (a kept work directory), `home` (the vibe home of `self update`); `total` — the size in bytes when the server announced it or the manifest declared it, absent otherwise and allowed to appear later; `started` — the wall-clock instant, RFC 3339 with milliseconds; `pid` and `command` — the process and the command line's verb (`install -g`, `cache add`, `self update`) that owns it; `batch` — the run the command belongs to, the run record's id for `install -g`, `update -g`, `modify` and `app`-driven installs (`PROP-065#runs`) and `<pid>` otherwise, so the transfers of one installation (its sources and its requirements' clones) group under one id; `precision` — `counted` when vibe counted bytes returned by its input reader, `reported` when it relayed what git reported (`#git`).

p.purpose: The purpose vocabulary is closed: `package-source` (a `[[sources]]` entry of an application installer option), `archive` (an `archive` step's input), `native-input` (a `native` step's input), `package-clone` (a registry's per-package clone for a project install, `install -g`'s requirement resolution or `cache add`), `release-bundle` (a vibe release of `self install|update`), `index-file` (a catalog file of an index: `repomd.json`, `by-name/*.json`, the primary), `other` (a download no row above names; a new kind of download amends this list before it ships). A reader groups by `package` for "one installation", by `purpose` for "what kind of traffic", and by `pid` for "one command".

p.sampling: A transfer produces a **sample** — `{at, bytes, rate_bps}` with `at` the wall clock in RFC 3339 with milliseconds, `bytes` the cumulative count and `rate_bps` the bytes of the last second divided by that second (0 for the first sample) — at its start (`bytes = 0`), then whenever 250 ms have passed since the previous sample or 1 MiB has arrived since it, whichever comes first, and at its end. The input reader settles a previous read at the next read or explicit terminal call. Input bytes alone do not prove successful disk writes; the independent optional counter of `#disk-writes` observes the owned writer. The cadence is a constant of the wrapper, not a flag: a finer cadence costs the stream and the journal more than a graph can show, a coarser one shows a stalled download late; the shell confirmed 250 ms against its one-bar-per-second graph.

p.disk-writes: An instrumented transfer additionally carries optional `disk_written_bytes`, a canonical unsigned decimal u64 string (PROP-044#M-WIDE-INTEGERS-AS-STRINGS), an exact cumulative count in bytes of successful logical `Write` return values at its owned unbuffered file writer. It starts at known zero when the writer is attached, not merely when a transfer or command starts; every successful short write contributes its returned count even if a later write, validation, sync, cancellation or cleanup fails. Failed/unperformed bytes contribute nothing. Rewrites count again; deleting a partial file never subtracts bytes. This is not network `bytes`, final retained `written`, physical disk I/O, flush/fsync success or operation-wide disk usage. Missing instrumentation, legacy records and unrepresentable overflow remain absent/unknown, never invented zero. A new transfer ID resets the count; `continues` does not carry an earlier counter. The owned writer and reader form one pair consumed before terminal reporting. The existing sampler copies this counter into each subsequent sample, active entry, listing last sample, watch event and terminal/history record; finish, fail, interruption and drop flush a final observation. Existing sampling cadence is retained; no independent timer/service or disk-rate field is introduced. Consumers derive rates from counter differences and timestamps, and deduplicate stream/watch by transfer ID; parent task counters are not aggregates and must not be summed with children. The first instrumented vertical is installer HTTP source/archive/native-input cache writes; memory-only index reads, uninstrumented release writers, native/external Git and local copy/extraction remain unknown. HTTP cache hits do not manufacture a transfer or zero-write record. Optional epoch-1 output evolution requires the explicit compatibility decision recorded in the format ledger; old permissive Rust readers may ignore the new field, but strict validators require updated schemas.

p.stream: For the tool that started the command, a transfer is a task of the progress stream of `PROP-060#MACHINE-STREAM` (`vibe-progress-event/1`, additive): every line of the transfer's task carries `transfer` = the id — the same one the journal uses, so a reader that listens to both glues them instead of doubling — and its `start` line carries beside it a `transfer_record` object with the fields of `#transfer` except `pid` and `command` (the stream's own process is known to its reader; one member cannot be an object on one line and a string on the next, which is why the record has a name of its own); the task is a child of the step that asked for the bytes; each sample is a `measurement` line with `completed = bytes`, `total` when known, `unit = "bytes"` and `rate_bps`, stamped as the sample is taken; its `finish` line carries `completed`, `total`, `transfer` and `peak_bps` as the final figures, and a `fail` line carries the same figures as far as it got with the message naming the cause (`interrupted` when the command was). No line computes a rate. Under the human renderer the transfer's task draws no row of its own: it is the running block of its step, with `12.40 MiB of 40.10 MiB · 2.10 MiB/s` as its metadata (`PROP-067#meta`, `PROP-065#display`), the bytes in the bar's own units and the rate the sample's `rate_bps`, so the screen and the stream agree.

p.journal: For any tool on the machine, the wrapper also keeps a **journal** under the settings root (`PROP-059#index` names the root): `transfers/active/<pid>-<n>.json` — the transfer's fields, `peak_bps` so far and its samples of the last five minutes, rewritten at every sample by writing a temporary file beside and renaming over (on Windows too — `MoveFileEx` with replace), removed at the end; `transfers/history.jsonl` — one line per finished or failed transfer, appended at the end, with the fields, the outcome (`finished` | `failed` with the message | `interrupted`), the totals (`bytes`, `elapsed_ms`, `average_bps`, `peak_bps` over one-second buckets) and `series` — the per-second buckets `[{second, bytes}]` from start to end, capped at 3600 entries (a longer transfer keeps one bucket per `ceil(n/3600)` seconds and says so in `bucket_seconds`); the file keeps the last 7 days or the last 500 entries, whichever is smaller, trimmed at each append; a `git` transfer's entry adds `written` — the size on disk after the clone — because its received bytes are reported, not counted (received bytes and logical writes remain separate even for a counted transfer); `transfers/revision` — a counter bumped at every change of the active set, the same device `PROP-059#launcher-runtime` uses so a watcher polls one small file. A process that dies leaves its active file behind; a reader treats an active file whose `pid` is gone (`PROP-059#launcher-runtime`'s liveness check) as `interrupted` and `vibe transfers` moves it to history on the next listing. The five-minute window is the screen's graph horizon; the 3600-bucket cap keeps a finished entry under a few tens of kilobytes.

p.verbs: `vibe transfers [--json]` lists the active transfers with their last sample and the recent history (newest first, the last 50 entries unless `--since <duration|timestamp>` names a window; `--package` takes `group/name` or a full key and `--purpose P` filters both sections) under protocol `vibe-transfers/1`; an active entry carries its last sample as `last`; it is the shell's downloads page in one document. `vibe transfers watch --json` first writes one `started` line, with the record and the last sample, for every transfer already active when it connects — a reader that attaches while downloads run, or after its own restart, misses nothing and never has to stitch a listing to a stream across a gap — then streams one line per sample of every active transfer and one line per change of the active set (`started`, `finished`, `failed`, `interrupted`), read from the journal every 250 ms, until its stdin closes (`vibe-transfer-event/1`); it never starts or stops a transfer. In every line `bytes` is the cumulative count since the transfer began, never an increment, and `total` is the record's. A transfer that begins and ends between two reads still gets its `started` line before its end, read from the history; like the listing, `watch` moves the active file of a gone process to the history and reports it `interrupted`. `vibe transfers history --json [--since] [--package]` is the history alone; `vibe transfers clear-history` empties it and closes with a trailer (`--json` answers the emptied listing). The human forms draw PROP-067 lists: a rule per section, one row per transfer with `package · purpose · 12.4 MB of 40.1 MB · 2.1 MB/s`, and the history with `bytes · time · average`. Nothing here asks; nothing here changes an installation.

p.limit: Every HTTP transfer goes through the one wrapper, so a rate limit is one token bucket there: `[transfer] limit = "5 MB/s"` in the user-level config (the file `PROP-030` names; the shell's Settings → Market writes it) applies to the sum of the process's HTTP transfers, read once at the composition root; `limit = "0"` or no key means none. A git transfer is not limited (git has no portable throttle a child's config honours) and its entry says `limited = false`; an HTTP entry under a limit says `limited = true` and names the figure in `limit_bps`. A limit that does not read (`"fast"`) is said once on stderr and ignored; units are decimal (`KB`, `MB`, `GB`) or binary (`KiB`, `MiB`, `GiB`), with or without `/s`. There is no flag: the limit is a machine setting, not a run's.

p.pause: A transfer is not paused on its own: a download belongs to the command that runs it, and the command is interrupted and resumed as `PROP-065#cancellation` and `#resume` say (`vibe app stop` for a launcher is a different thing). An interrupted transfer's history entry says `interrupted` and names the command's resume line in `resume`, so a downloads screen can offer "Resume" without knowing the command; a resumed download is a new transfer whose entry names the previous one in `continues`. Partial files are the step's business (`PROP-065#sources` keeps or discards them); the journal does not promise that bytes already received are reused.

p.coverage: The wrapper is `vibe_core::progress::transfer` (a reader adapter over any `Read` plus the task and the journal), and these places use it: the fetch of `[[sources]]`, `archive` and `native` inputs in `vibe-app` (`installer/fetch.rs`), the release download of `self install|update` (`vvm/bundle/download.rs`), and the catalog files of the index client (`vibe-registry/index_client`, journaled once the resolver holding the client receives the invocation's progress). A new download that does not go through the wrapper is a defect.

p.coverage-git: The git clone and fetch of the registry backend (`git_backend/shell/checkout.rs`, through `shell/reported.rs`) use it through `#git`. A test (`vibe-cli`, `composition/transfers/coverage_tests.rs`) lists every file of `crates/*/src` that sends an HTTP request or begins a counted transfer, and every argument list that runs `git clone` or `git fetch`, and names each as wrapped or exempt with one line of why: the publish side, which uploads; the LLM transport, which is not a download; the doc shell's fetch; the aiui control client; the remap probe's HEAD requests; the index scanner of `vibe-index`, which runs on a server; the VVM build pipeline's checkout of vibe's own source; and the metadata reads of resolution and search (the single-manifest HTTPS read that stands in for `git archive`, the index handshake and per-package lookups, `search --full-scan`). A new reader fails the test until it is wrapped or listed, and a listed one that is wrapped or gone fails it too.

p.git: A clone or fetch runs the git binary; vibe adds `--progress` and reads git's lines on stderr as they arrive, split on `\r` and `\n` (`Receiving objects: 45% (900/2000), 12.30 MiB | 2.10 MiB/s`, or `Unpacking objects:` for a fetch small enough that git unpacks it loose), turning each line that names a size into a sample whose `bytes` is git's reported figure scaled from its binary unit, so the sample is `precision: "reported"` and its `total` is unknown until git says `100%` (the final figure becomes `total`); `Resolving deltas` adds no bytes, and a clone that recurses into submodules adds each repository's pass to the ones before. Git prints at its own cadence, about every 100 ms while bytes move; vibe does not smooth it. The transfer begins with git's first sized line and is dated from the start of the git process, so a fetch that moves nothing leaves no transfer and the bytes before the first line are not drawn as a burst. The transfer's `url` is the remote, reduced (`safe_remote`: a URL as `#redaction` says, the user of an scp-like remote removed, a local path as it is); `purpose` is `package-clone`, or `index-file` for an index served from a git host; `package` is `group/name` when the task that observes the clone knows it, and the transfer is that task's child on the stream. Its history entry adds `written`, the size of the repository's `.git/objects` after the operation, and says `limited: false`. The progress lines stay out of the stderr an error reports.

p.redaction: A transfer never records a credential: the URL is written through the same reduction `self update` already uses (`safe_url`: user, password, query and fragment removed), the journal is `0600` on Unix, and a `remap`-rewritten source (`PROP-066`) records the URL actually fetched, not the one the manifest named, with `remapped_from` naming the latter so a reader can show both.

p.display: In the terminal nothing new is drawn by default: the running step's block shows `12.4 MB of 40.1 MB · 2.1 MB/s` as today, and `vibe transfers` is the listing a user asks for. Under `--plain` a transfer leaves its end line only, as a child of its step's block (the plain renderer writes every block once, when it ends); the run log keeps no line of it. The desktop shell draws the graph; The shell's Activity screen (Architect, R127) draws, from `vibe transfers watch --json`, a NETWORK tile (the latest `rate_bps` summed over active transfers), a PEAK tile (the operation's peak), a per-second graph over the last five minutes normalised to the peak, and a byte line `Downloading data · 121.4 MB / 2.2 GB` with its own bar and ETA beside the operation's step percentage; at rest, the same tiles at zero and the day's totals (bytes, downloads) from the history; per-transfer rows stay in the step panel. The ETA and the day's sums are the shell's arithmetic.

p.schemas: `transfer_record.jtd.json` (the fields of `#transfer` with `limit_bps` beside `limited`, the `resume` line and `continues` of `#pause`, the outcome and totals of `#journal`, `series`, and the `last` sample a listing adds), `transfers_listing.jtd.json` (`vibe-transfers/1`: `{protocol, home, active: [record + last sample], history: [record]}`), `transfer_event.jtd.json` (`vibe-transfer-event/1`: `{protocol, at, event: sample | started | finished | failed | interrupted, id, batch, bytes?, total?, rate_bps?, peak_bps?, record?}` — `record` on `started`, the totals on the three ends), and, on `progress_event.jtd.json`, `transfer` (the id) on every line of a transfer's task, the `transfer_record` object on its `start`, `rate_bps` on `measurement`, and `peak_bps` on `finish`/`fail`. The active file is a `transfer_record` with `samples: [{at, bytes, rate_bps, disk_written_bytes?}]`; the optional disk counter also appears on progress measurements/ends, transfer records and watch events. It retains the separate meaning specified in `#disk-writes`. The three record definitions are one shape written three times, since a JTD document cannot refer to another.

p.acceptance: A fixture HTTP server that serves a 16 MiB body at a throttled rate; `vibe install -g` of a package whose `[[sources]]` names it, under `--progress-format json`: the `start` line carries the `transfer` object, the `measurement` lines arrive at the cadence with monotonic `bytes` and `at`, the `finish` line carries the total; during the run `vibe transfers --json` from another process lists it with a last sample no older than 500 ms, and `vibe transfers watch --json` streams its samples; after it, `history.jsonl` has one entry with `series` whose sum equals `bytes`; a killed process leaves an active file that the next listing turns into an `interrupted` entry; `[transfer] limit` holds the average within 20 % of the limit over the run; and a run that downloads nothing leaves no journal (`crates/vibe-cli/tests/cli_transfers.rs`).

p.acceptance-git: A `git+file://` per-package registry carrying a few hundred KiB of incompressible bytes; `vibe cache add` of its package under `--progress-format json`: a `start` line whose `transfer_record` says `kind: "git"`, `precision: "reported"`, beneath the package's own row, `measurement` lines with `rate_bps`, a `finish` line with the total; the history entry says `reported` with `written > 0`; a second warm-up, whose fetch moves nothing, adds no transfer (`crates/vibe-cli/tests/cli_transfers.rs`, and the backend alone in `crates/vibe-registry/tests/git_transfers.rs`); the coverage test of `#coverage-git` names every reader of a response body.

p.decisions: **Samples, not rates.** A rate depends on the window; two tools computing it the same way from the same samples agree, two tools reading a rate vibe chose do not. **Two sinks from one wrapper.** The attached stream serves the runner; the journal serves the machine, like Steam's downloads page shows every download whoever started it. **The journal is files, not a daemon.** The shell polls `revision` as it does for launchers; no socket, no service. **Git is reported, not counted.** Reading git's progress is honest about its precision; counting pack bytes ourselves would mean a git implementation in vibe. **No pause of a transfer alone.** The command owns the download; interrupt and resume already exist and the journal names the resume line.

p.proxy: **The network route.** One `[proxy]` table — in `~/.vibe/config.toml` or a site profile (`PROP-019#site-profile`), key by key the user's over the site's — decides how every connection vibe itself makes leaves the machine: `mode = "explicit"` (the `https` / `http` proxy URLs), `"px"` (a vibe-managed px, `#proxy-px`) or `"none"` (no proxy, whatever else is set; px keys stay and are simply unused). Absent, the mode is `explicit` when a proxy URL is set and no proxy otherwise: a proxy is an option, never a default, and px is never enabled without `mode = "px"`. The mode switches at every layer, highest first: `VIBEVM_PROXY_MODE=px|explicit|none`, the user's file, the site profile — so a user can turn a site's px off. `no_proxy` lists domain suffixes (`corp.example` and `.corp.example` cover the domain and below), exact hosts, IP addresses and CIDR ranges; loopback always connects directly. The decision is made in `vibe_core::net` and acted on by one owner, `vibe-net`: every `reqwest` client vibe builds (the controlled source transport, release and payload downloads, the LLM transport, the GitHub/GitVerse/index APIs, the documentation shell, remap probes, `xtask`) is configured there, and every child `git` that talks to an HTTP(S) remote receives the route explicitly (`#proxy-git`). Under source policy (`PROP-073#HTTP-ADMISSION`) a controlled client tunnels HTTPS through the proxy by `CONNECT` and sends plain HTTP in absolute form; admission judges the **requested host name** before the proxy is asked, since through a proxy the peer address is the proxy's — an excluded host is refused without contacting the proxy, and redirects are admitted hop by hop as before. A controlled client never inherits an ambient `HTTPS_PROXY` that is not the configured route. A transfer record names the proxy its connection went through (`proxy`: `scheme://host:port`, never a credential, or `px`; absent for a direct connection). Without `[proxy]` nothing changes. SSH remotes are not proxied: their route is the SSH client's own configuration. A long-lived `vibe` process (`vibe mcp`, `vibe app` launchers) follows the same rule for its own requests: its one operation is the process, so a managed px it starts lives until the process ends. The separately deployed `vibe-index` server installs no route: its scanner's requests keep the ambient `HTTPS_PROXY` environment (and the operating system's trust store), and it never starts px. Other children vibe starts (hooks, build tools) receive `HTTPS_PROXY` / `HTTP_PROXY` / `NO_PROXY` only in explicit mode, through the promoted environment; a managed px's address is not exported to them.

p.proxy-trust:
**Trust.** The operating system decides first, through its **own certificate verifier** (`rustls-platform-verifier`), one construction point for every TLS client vibe builds — downloads, `vibe dl`, the `--test-proxy` probe, the px reachability check, the registry HTTP clients, the release fetch. On Windows that is the CryptoAPI chain engine: **every** store the machine and the logged-in user have, the intermediate `CA` stores included, enterprise policy, and AIA issuer fetching — so a chain Edge builds is a chain vibe builds, which the earlier root-store-only reading could not do for a corporate chain whose subordinate authority is deployed to `CA`. On macOS it is the Security framework. Elsewhere it is webpki over the platform's root bundle, and there — and only there, since Windows and macOS run a root programme of their own, including the roots they distrust — vibe also still consults the public roots it ships, so a minimal container that installs no CA bundle keeps working. Revocation keeps the semantics `#proxy-revocation` names for a child git: the Windows engine checks the end certificate and accepts one whose state could not be retrieved (`CERT_CHAIN_REVOCATION_CHECK_END_CERT` with `CERT_CHAIN_POLICY_IGNORE_ALL_REV_UNKNOWN_FLAGS`), which is `best-effort`; vibe's own rustls clients perform no online revocation check, as before.
**Extra certificates, always additive.** `[tls] extra_ca` — one path or a list of them, each a certificate file (PEM, one or many, or a single DER) or a **directory**, whose `*.pem`, `*.crt` and `*.cer` files are all read in name order — is trusted **in addition to** the operating system's decision, never instead of it. `[proxy] ca_file` is the older spelling of the same thing, keeps working unchanged, and is simply the first entry of the effective list; the two are merged without repeats, and each layers on its own key (the user's file over the site profile). A certificate authority among them becomes an extra trust anchor, which is how an intermediate the server never sends can complete a chain. Any certificate among them, authority or not, also becomes a **pin**: webpki will not take an end-entity certificate as a trust anchor, so a self-signed server certificate is trusted only by naming its own bytes — and then only when the presented leaf's DER is exactly those bytes, the certificate is current, and it is for the host being contacted (`subjectAltName`, or the common name when the certificate carries no `subjectAltName` at all; one leading wildcard label). An expired pin and a pin for another name are refused.
Verification is never switched off and no key disables it. A named file that cannot be read, holds no certificate, or is a directory with no certificate file in it is a configuration error naming the path and the fix. An untrusted server certificate fails as such (`unable to get local issuer` / `UnknownIssuer`), names the issuer the chain ended at, says who refused it (the system store alone, or the system store and the extra certificates), and its fix says how to export that issuer **on this operating system** — the PowerShell export over `Root` and `CA` of both `CurrentUser` and `LocalMachine` on Windows, `security find-certificate` on macOS, the distribution's CA directory elsewhere — and which key to name it in. A report says which part of the trust set accepted a chain: `trusted by system`, `trusted by extra CA: <file>`, or `pinned self-signed: <file>`.

p.proxy-git: **Child git.** A child `git` that contacts an HTTP(S) remote — a URL among its arguments, or the URL of the named remote a `fetch`/`pull`/`push`/`ls-remote` reads from its repository — receives `-c http.proxy=<proxy>` (empty for a bypassed host, which disables proxying for that child), `HTTPS_PROXY`/`HTTP_PROXY`/`NO_PROXY` (the configured list plus loopback) and, when extra certificates are configured at all, `-c http.sslCAInfo=<bundle>`. A child `git` cannot be handed a verifier, only a file, and on Windows that file **replaces** the certificate store rather than adding to it — Git's own documentation of `http.schannelUseSSLCAInfo` says the bundle "would override the Windows Certificate Store" — so the bundle carries this machine's own certificates first and the configured ones after: on Windows everything in `ROOT` **and** `CA` of both `CurrentUser` and `LocalMachine` (the earlier bundle read only `CurrentUser\ROOT`, which is exactly why a corporate chain ending at a subordinate authority could not be completed from it), elsewhere the platform bundle. Windows keeps schannel as the backend, named explicitly (`-c http.sslBackend=schannel -c http.schannelUseSSLCAInfo=true`): it is the stack every other Windows application uses, and `http.sslBackend=openssl` is documented as ignored when the build's libcurl cannot choose a backend at runtime, which would fail silently. With nothing configured no bundle is passed and the child uses the platform's own trust, which on Windows is the whole store. The bundle is content-addressed in `<settings-dir>/tls/<sha256>.pem`, written through a temporary file in the same directory, so it outlives the call that wrote it, two runs of the same trust set write one file, and a stale file can never be read as a current trust set. A proxy URL carrying a credential is passed only through the environment, never on the command line. The controlled native transport (`PROP-073#NATIVE-PREPARATION`) receives the same route in place of its fixed empty `http.proxy`. The user's git configuration is never written. A local-only git call receives nothing and never starts px.

p.proxy-px: **Managed px.** With `mode = "px"`, vibe starts px (https://github.com/genotrance/px, MIT) itself: lazily, at the first request or git child of an operation that needs a non-bypassed connection — a command with no network need never starts it — on a free `127.0.0.1` port (or the fixed `[proxy] px_port`; busy is an error naming the holder when observable, never another port), as `px --listen=127.0.0.1 --port=N --foreground=1` plus the route: `pac` — an `http(s)://` URL px fetches (it must be reachable without the proxy it configures), an absolute file path or `file:///…`, or `system` (spelled `system`, alias `windows`: whatever proxy configuration this operating system is configured with — the logged-in Windows user's Internet Options, the macOS network settings, or the Linux desktops and the environment — read by vibe and handed to px explicitly, `#proxy-system`) — or `upstream = "host:port"` (`--proxy`), the bypass list (`--noproxy`) and the site's `px_args` (arguments vibe owns are refused). `VIBEVM_PROXY_PAC` overrides `pac` over the user's file over the site profile. Readiness is the port accepting connections (20 s). One px serves the whole operation; it is an operation resource of the invocation's cancellation token (`PROP-073#OPERATION-EFFECTS-LAW`) and is killed and reaped when the operation ends — success, error, a stop file or Ctrl-C. On Unix px runs under a `/bin/sh` supervisor in its own process group whose stdin pipe only vibe holds, so even a vibe killed outright leaves no px; on Windows px runs in a job object that kills it when vibe exits, in its own console process group so an attended Ctrl-C question does not stop it first. A px that cannot serve is reported once with its cause — not installed (where vibe looked), failed to start, exited (its last output), not ready, port busy — and how to turn px off; the request is sent to an unresolvable address rather than silently going direct. px is located as `[proxy] px_path` when set, else `tools/px/` beside the running vibe (or its parent directory), else `px` on PATH. A distribution carries px as `tools/px/` with px's `LICENSE.txt` and a `NOTICE` line: `xtask/dist/px.toml` pins the version, the per-target asset URL and SHA-256, and `cargo xtask dist px --target T` fetches, verifies and lays it out (macOS x86_64 has no upstream asset: a system px through `pip install px-proxy` and `px_path`).

p.proxy-system: **`pac = "system"` is resolved by vibe, never by px.** px given no `--pac` detects the Windows proxy configuration itself, and on a managed desktop that detection finds nothing: the PAC URL lives inside the `DefaultConnectionSettings` blob of the user's `Connections` key and the plain `AutoConfigURL` value is often absent, so every request through such a px goes nowhere. With `pac = "system"` (alias `windows`; `system` is the canonical spelling and what every report prints) vibe therefore reads the logged-in user's configuration itself and starts px with the explicit `--pac=<url>`, or `--proxy=<host:port>` when the configuration names a fixed proxy instead. The answer is read per operation, when px starts — the settings may have changed since the last one, and the reads are a few registry lookups and one WinHTTP call — and the setting that answered is reported beside it. The order is a law, first hit wins: (1) the group-policy auto-config URL, `HKCU\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Internet Settings` value `AutoConfigURL`, then `HKLM` at the same path; (2) the user's configuration as Windows itself exposes it, `WinHttpGetIEProxyConfigForCurrentUser` (`fAutoDetect`, `lpszAutoConfigUrl`, `lpszProxy`, `lpszProxyBypass`), which covers the `Connections` blob — and, only when that call fails or answers nothing usable, the `AutoConfigURL` value under `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Internet Settings` and then that key's `Connections\DefaultConnectionSettings` blob parsed directly (little-endian `u32` version, `u32` change counter, `u32` flags — `0x1` direct, `0x2` proxy, `0x4` auto-config URL, `0x8` auto-detect — then three length-prefixed ASCII strings: the proxy server, the bypass list, the auto-config URL; a URL whose flag is off is stale and ignored, as Windows ignores it); (3) auto-detection alone, `fAutoDetect` with no URL, resolved with `WinHttpDetectAutoProxyConfigUrl(WINHTTP_AUTO_DETECT_TYPE_DHCP | WINHTTP_AUTO_DETECT_TYPE_DNS_A)`; (4) no PAC but a configured proxy server, taken as px's `--proxy` (`https=` preferred over `http=` over a bare `host:port`; `socks` and `ftp` are not routes px can take) together with that setting's bypass list, which becomes px's `--noproxy` when `[proxy] no_proxy` names none — a configured `no_proxy` or `upstream` is the user's own word and outranks what Windows said; (5) nothing found: px is not started and the refusal names every setting that was read, with what each said, and the fix (`pac = "<your PAC URL>"`, an absolute PAC file path, or `upstream = "host:port"`). A reader that fails is reported among the settings checked, never swallowed. The order logic, the blob parser and the proxy-string reduction are pure functions over an injected Windows-settings seam, so they are tested on every host and no test depends on the machine it runs on; only the reader behind the seam is Windows. **Auto means something on every host.** A corporate profile exists per operating system in the same three variants — manual (an explicit `upstream`), pac (an explicit PAC URL) and auto (`pac = "system"`: take whatever the operating system is configured with) — so the Windows order above has two siblings, built exactly the same way: an ordered set of sources, the first that yields a configuration wins, each reported by name, every step a pure function over an injected seam and only the reader behind it per-OS. `pac = "system"` is therefore accepted on every host and carries no `vibe self apply` warning; a host that is neither Windows, macOS nor another Unix has no configuration to read and refuses, naming the two ways out. On **macOS** the source is the system proxy configuration of the current network service as `SCDynamicStoreCopyProxies` reports it — the dictionary `scutil --proxy` prints, which is how the reader obtains it: `ProxyAutoConfigEnable` with `ProxyAutoConfigURLString` is the PAC URL; `ProxyAutoDiscoveryEnable` is WPAD (below); `HTTPSEnable` with `HTTPSProxy` and `HTTPSPort`, else the `HTTP*` triple, is px's `--proxy` (a service with no port is reported as `:80`, as macOS itself shows it); `ExceptionsList` is the bypass list. An `…Enable` that is off is ignored exactly as macOS ignores it, so a stale URL left by a switched-off profile never becomes the route. The environment (below) is the last source, and then the refusal. On **Linux and the other Unixes** the order is: (1) the GNOME / GTK desktop, `org.gnome.system.proxy` as `gsettings list-recursively` prints it — `mode 'auto'` is `autoconfig-url` (empty: WPAD), `mode 'manual'` is the `https` child's `host`/`port` else the `http` child's, `ignore-hosts` is the bypass list, every other mode is no configuration; (2) the KDE desktop, `[Proxy Settings]` of `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/kioslaverc` — `ProxyType` 2 is `Proxy Config Script`, 3 is WPAD, 1 is `httpsProxy` else `httpProxy` (KDE's `http://host port` spelling included), 4 defers to the environment, `NoProxyFor` is the bypass list; (3) the environment — `https_proxy` / `HTTPS_PROXY`, then `http_proxy` / `HTTP_PROXY`, then `all_proxy` / `ALL_PROXY`, each reduced to `host:port` so a credential in the value is dropped rather than printed, with `no_proxy` as the bypass list; a loopback value is skipped, because that is vibe's own px and px pointed at itself is a loop; (4) nothing found: px is not started and the refusal names every source that was looked at with what each said, and the two ways out. **WPAD** answers a source that asks to auto-discover, on the spot, before the next source is read: for each of the host's DNS search domains and its FQDN (`/etc/resolv.conf` `search` / `domain`) vibe generates `http://wpad.<domain>/wpad.dat`, walking up the labels, and fetches them in order — directly, as a PAC URL must be reachable without the proxy it configures, with a bounded timeout each — taking the first that answers `200` with a body declaring `FindProxyForURL`. The walk **never reaches a public suffix**: it stops while at least two labels remain, so `wpad.example.com` is asked and `wpad.com` is not, and at most six candidates are ever generated. A discovery that finds nothing is reported and the order continues to the next source. Every report prints the same phrase with the source named — `system → https://pac.example.corp/proxy.pac (from GNOME settings)`, `system → proxy proxy.example.corp:8080 · bypass *.corp.example (from macOS network settings)`, `… (from environment https_proxy)`, `… (from WPAD discovery)` — at `vibe self apply --show`, `vibe self doctor --network` and `vibe dl --test-proxy`. A test seam, for the same reason the pure functions exist: `$VIBEVM_SYSTEM_PROXY_FIXTURE` names a directory whose `gsettings`, `kioslaverc`, `scutil-proxy`, `dns-domains` and `wpad` files stand in for this machine's desktop, and `$VIBEVM_SYSTEM_PROXY_OS` (`unix` / `macos` / `windows`) names the order to run, so a whole `vibe` can be driven over a stated configuration on any host and no test touches the developer's own desktop. Unset, both change nothing.

p.proxy-revocation: **Certificate revocation on Windows.** A corporate TLS-inspecting proxy re-signs every certificate with its own CA, and that CA's CRL and OCSP distribution points usually live outside the network it inspects. Windows schannel then cannot complete the revocation lookup and fails the handshake — the failure `curl` needs `--ssl-no-revoke` to get past. `[proxy] revocation` decides what vibe asks of a child `git` whose TLS runs through schannel: `check` (the default, and exactly what vibe did before the key existed — nothing is added to the child), `best-effort` (revocation is checked, but a certificate whose state could not be retrieved is accepted; one the CA says is revoked is still refused) or `off` (no revocation check at all). It switches at every layer, highest first: `VIBEVM_PROXY_REVOCATION=check|best-effort|off`, the user's file, the site profile. The chain itself is always verified against the trust set of `#proxy-trust`; no key disables that. `off` adds `-c http.schannelCheckRevoke=false` (libcurl `CURLSSLOPT_NO_REVOKE`) and `best-effort` adds `-c http.schannelCheckRevoke=best-effort` (`CURLSSLOPT_REVOKE_BEST_EFFORT`), which is Git for Windows' own third value for that key from 2.26 — an upstream git parses the key as a boolean and would refuse the word, so the word is sent only to a git that reports a Git for Windows 2.26 or newer (`git --version`, asked at most once per process and only for `best-effort` on Windows) and otherwise falls back to `off` with a note. git applies the key only when `http.sslBackend` is `schannel`; vibe never writes that choice, so a git built against OpenSSL is unaffected, as is every non-Windows host, where the setting adds nothing. vibe's own HTTP clients are rustls and perform no online revocation check, so the setting does not reach them and none of them needs it. px is unaffected too: px's libcurl uses schannel on Windows but exposes no revocation option at all, and for an HTTPS target px only tunnels (`CONNECT`), so the handshake that can fail this way is the client's own — which is where the setting applies. A failure that looks like one — `CRYPT_E_NO_REVOCATION_CHECK` / `0x80092012`, `CRYPT_E_REVOCATION_OFFLINE` / `0x80092013`, or a message about the revocation function being unable to check — is classified as `revocation` by the diagnosis of `#proxy-doctor` and by `vibe dl`'s classifier (which reports it as a TLS failure, `dl_tls`, exit 13), and the fix it prints names this key.

p.proxy-doctor: **Diagnosis.** `vibe self doctor` checks the route when `[proxy]` configures a proxy or a CA file, or when `--network [URL]` asks (default `https://github.com/`), in order, stopping at the first step the rest depend on: the trust set (how many certificates the operating system's own stores hold, and how many extra authorities and pins the configured files add), the PAC (fetched directly or read; `system` is resolved first and the row names the URL px will be given and the Windows setting it came from, or, when the settings name a fixed proxy, that proxy — a resolution that finds nothing is the failed row, with every setting it read), `px --test=<target>`, `CONNECT` through the proxy (`407` = the request is not going through px / single sign-on), TLS with the trust set (`unable to get local issuer` = the CA; a timeout = a blocked direct route). Each failed step names its cause and fix; `--json` carries the rows under `network`. `vibe self apply --show` prints the effective mode and PAC with the layer each came from, every `[proxy]` key, the whole effective extra-certificate list (`extra_ca`, both spellings merged), what `pac = "system"` resolved to here (`pac_resolved`) and, when a layer asked for one, the revocation setting of `#proxy-revocation` with its layer (`revocation`, `revocation_origin`). `vibe dl --test-proxy`'s `pac` row carries the same resolution phrase — `system → https://… (from user Internet Options)` — and its `config` row the revocation setting when it is not the default.

p.proxy-tool: **vibe's px, lent to another tool.** A network that needs px needs it for `pip`, `npm`, `cargo` and `curl` too, and each of those has its own idea of how a proxy is configured; px is the one thing on the machine that knows how to authenticate here. `vibe tool px exec [--port N] [--env NAME=VALUE]… [--proxy-env NAME]… [--allow-direct] -- <command> [args…]` therefore starts exactly the px vibe's own operations start — the same effective `[proxy]` table and its layers, the same `pac` resolution including `#proxy-system`, the same `upstream`, `px_port`, `px_args` and `px_path`, the same companion lookup of `PROP-019#companion-tools`, and the same lifetime: px is the invocation's operation resource, killed and reaped by the supervisor (Unix) or job object (Windows) when the invocation ends, which is after the child has exited, whichever way it exited. The command is resolved on `PATH` as the operating system resolves it (on Windows with `PATHEXT`, and never the bare extensionless name); a name carrying a separator is a path and is run as written; a name that is not there is reported by name before px starts, and the exit is **127** — the shell's own code for it, which a wrapper's caller tests for, not vibe's refusal exit. The child receives `HTTPS_PROXY`, `https_proxy`, `HTTP_PROXY` and `http_proxy` — all four, because the tools that need px disagree about which they read — set to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>`, and `NO_PROXY` / `no_proxy` set to loopback followed by `[proxy] no_proxy`, the same list vibe hands its own children. `--proxy-env NAME` additionally sets `NAME` to that URL, for a tool that reads its own name for the proxy (`npm_config_proxy`, `PIP_PROXY`) and cannot be told the address in advance; `--env NAME=VALUE` adds a literal variable and is applied last, so a caller can override any of the above. stdin, stdout, stderr and the terminal's signals are the child's: vibe writes nothing to them, so `exec` can stand inside a pipeline (`pxpip freeze > requirements.txt` holds the child's bytes and nothing else), and what vibe has to say about the route it lent is said on stderr only under `--verbose`. **The child's exit code is vibe's** — a wrapper around `exec` fails exactly as the tool it wraps does; a child that died on a signal answers 130 when the invocation was stopped and 1 otherwise. `mode = "explicit"` lends the configured proxy URL as the table wrote it instead — a bare `http://host:port` is handed over without the trailing path parsing would add, so the child reports the proxy its administrator configured — and starts no px, since starting one would add a hop nobody asked for (a credential in that URL travels in the environment, never in a printed line). No proxy configured at all is a refusal, because `exec` is asked for precisely when the child cannot reach the network by itself; `--allow-direct` runs the child anyway, with the proxy variables removed rather than inherited. `vibe tool px serve [--port N] [--json]` runs px in the foreground until the invocation is stopped, printing the listen address, the resolved PAC or upstream and the bypass list (`vibe-px-serve/1`), for a tool vibe cannot start itself; `vibe tool px status` is `vibe self px status` under the name a user of `vibe tool px` already has in hand. Both verbs accept `--stop-file`.

p.dl: **`vibe dl <url> <dest>`.** One `http://` / `https://` file through exactly the stack of every other download: the operation's source policy and controlled transport, the route of `#proxy` (with nothing configured, no proxy: a proxy is an option, never a default), the managed px of `#proxy-px` started and reaped for this operation, the trust set of `#proxy-trust`. Remap rows are not applied — `dl` fetches the URL it is given, so the route it reports is that URL's. `<dest>` is a file or an existing directory (the URL's last segment); an existing file needs `--force`; bytes go to a temporary file beside it, verified (`--sha256`), then renamed; a failure or a stop removes the partial file. `--show` prints the body byte-exact on stdout, `--headers` the status line and headers (alone: a GET whose body is not printed; both: headers, a blank line, the body); a binary body is refused on a terminal unless `--force`; every diagnostic goes to stderr and no request credential, cookie or proxy authorization is ever printed (`Set-Cookie` values are redacted). `--proxy` turns a proxy on for this command only: bare (px with the configured `pac` / `upstream`), `px`, `pac=<url|file|system>`, or a proxy URL. Before the transfer a diagnostic probe walks the route with its own connection and never sends a request to a server the trust set does not accept: the route decision and its origin, the `no_proxy` match, DNS (direct route), the proxy's `CONNECT` status line, TLS version, cipher, the server's chain (subject and issuer, so an inspecting CA is visible) and the trust source that accepted it (`system`, `extra_ca` or `pinned`, with the file in `trusted_by_source` for the latter two), the response head and each redirect (`-v`: chain and redirect headers), with per-phase timings; `--json` is `vibe-dl/1` (`schemas/dl_report.jtd.json`). Each failure is classified with its cause and fix and exits distinctly: 1 not HTTP / other, 2 usage, 3 `--offline`, 4 source policy, 5 px, 6 DNS, 7 connect timeout (a direct route where only a proxy may leave), 8 connection refused, 9 proxy `407`, 10 `CONNECT` refused, 11 untrusted certificate (`unable to get local issuer`, the issuer named), 12 name mismatch, 13 other TLS, 14 HTTP 4xx, 15 HTTP 5xx, 16 SHA-256 mismatch, 17 destination exists, 18 local I/O, 19 binary body on a terminal, 20 redirect refused (downgrade, loop), 130 stopped. `vibe dl --test-proxy [<url>]` (default `https://gmail.com`, redirects followed) checks the configured proxy step by step instead of downloading — the effective mode and its origin, the `[proxy]` layers, the `no_proxy` match, the PAC source and whether it was read (the per-target PAC answer is not exposed by px), px present / started / `px --test`, the route, `CONNECT`, TLS trust, the HTTP answer — continuing past a failure where the next step can still be judged; on failure a `Check │ Result │ Cause │ Fix` table names every problem and the exit is 21 for a proxy problem, 22 for a target problem; `--no-px` tests the explicit or upstream proxy without px.
